strengths: Addresses a timely and well-motivated problem: reducing the cost of evaluating candidate agentic workflows by learning a predictor rather than relying on repeated LLM executions, analogous to performance predictors in NAS.

The multi-view encoding design (graph, code, prompt) is intuitively well-justified given the heterogeneous nature of agentic workflow configurations, and the cross-domain unsupervised pretraining strategy is a reasonable approach to mitigate label scarcity.

Reasonably thorough experimental suite: main accuracy/utility comparisons across three domains, ablations on views and graph variants, a low-label-ratio study, and an appendix on downstream workflow optimization and transferability, plus qualitative case studies.
Consistent (though sometimes modest) improvements over graph-based and MLP baselines across domains, particularly in low-label regimes, supporting the claimed benefit of pretraining.
Clear positioning relative to concurrent work (FLORA-Bench, MAS-GPT) with an explicit comparison table of design choices.
weaknesses: Benchmark scope is narrow: only the AFlow subset of FLORA-Bench is used, with very small numbers of unique workflows per domain (30-42), raising concerns about the statistical robustness and generalizability of the reported gains.

No baseline comparison against the actual GNN predictor proposed conceptually in FLORA-Bench or against MAS-GPT, despite both being discussed at length as the closest related work; comparisons are only made to generic GNN architectures (GCN, GAT, etc.) not designed for this task.

Ablation results (Table 4) show unstable and sometimes counterintuitive behavior across view combinations (e.g., large performance collapses for certain two-view combinations on reasoning tasks), which is not analyzed or explained, undermining confidence in the multi-view design's robustness.
Utility improvements are inconsistent across domains—the model is only second-best (behind GCN) on reasoning task utility—weakening the claim of uniform state-of-the-art performance.

The technical contribution is largely a combination of established techniques (multi-view fusion, contrastive+reconstruction pretraining, GNN/MLP encoders) adapted from the NAS predictor literature, with limited fundamental novelty in method design.

The workflow-optimization experiment in the appendix is fairly limited: only random search with predictor-based reranking is tested, without stronger search integration or clearer accounting of trade-offs versus full search-based baselines beyond raw accuracy numbers.
Minor presentation issues (e.g., typo 'Codi Generation' in Table 4, some inconsistent notation) suggest the manuscript could benefit from another editing pass.

strengths: The paper identifies a legitimate and timely problem: the high cost of evaluating candidate agentic workflows during automated design/search, and proposes a predictor-based alternative analogous to NAS performance predictors.

The multi-view encoding idea (graph + code + prompt) is a sensible extension over the single-view GNN baseline (FLORA-Bench), and the paper provides ablations (Tables 4-5) that at least attempt to isolate the contribution of each view.

The cross-domain unsupervised pretraining strategy targeting label scarcity is a reasonable direction, and the low-label-ratio experiments (Figure 3/4) show the predictor+pretraining variant degrades more gracefully than baselines.

The paper includes an extended appendix with a workflow-optimization experiment (Table 6) and case studies showing qualitative examples of optimized workflows, which is a nice attempt to connect prediction accuracy to downstream utility.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to a single benchmark (FLORA-Bench, AFlow subset only) with a very small number of distinct workflows per domain (30-42), raising serious concerns about the generality and statistical robustness of the reported accuracy/utility gains.

The improvements over baselines are modest and inconsistent: GCN actually beats Agentic Predictor on reasoning-task utility (91.82 vs 91.47), and several ablation configurations show erratic/unstable behavior (e.g., graph+text view combination drops accuracy to 54.17% on reasoning tasks in Table 4), which is not explained and undermines confidence in the reported architecture choices.

Novelty is limited: the core idea largely amounts to adding code/prompt MLP encoders and reconstruction+contrastive pretraining on top of the existing single-view GNN predictor from FLORA-Bench (a concurrent work explicitly cited as inspiration for the graph encoder), rather than introducing a fundamentally new technique. The claim to be 'the first predictive framework' is undercut by acknowledging two contemporaneous works (FLORA-Bench, MAS-GPT) tackling essentially the same goal.

The reported '$0.00 search cost' for Agentic Predictor in Table 6 is misleading: training the predictor still requires a labeled dataset of executed workflows (with ground-truth performance), whose collection cost is not accounted for anywhere in the comparison, overstating the practical efficiency advantage.

Baselines for the main comparison (MLP, GCN, GAT, GCN-II, Graph Transformer, One-For-All) are all generic graph/NAS-style predictors inherited wholesale from the benchmark paper; there is no comparison against other plausible predictor designs (e.g., LLM-based fine-tuning as in MAS-GPT) despite discussing them in related work, weakening the empirical positioning claimed in Table 1.

The relationship between the main results (Table 3) and the pretraining variant (Agentic Predictor+) is unclear—it is not explicitly stated whether Table 3's headline numbers include pretraining, making it hard to assess how much of the improvement stems from multi-view encoding alone versus pretraining.

Transferability results (Appendix A.3) are weak on HotpotQA (13.37%, underperforming baselines), which somewhat contradicts the claimed robustness/generalizability, and this negative result is understated in the discussion.
The problem formulation treats performance as binary pass/fail, which is a substantial simplification for many realistic agentic tasks; this limitation is acknowledged but not addressed empirically.

strengths: Addresses a practical and timely problem: the high computational/financial cost of evaluating candidate agentic workflows during automated design/search.

The multi-view encoding idea (graph/topology, code, prompt) is well-motivated and empirically validated through careful ablations (Tables 4-5), showing each view and the multi-graph design contributes to performance.

Cross-domain unsupervised pretraining (Agentic Predictor+) is shown to meaningfully help in low-label regimes (Fig. 3-4), which is a practically relevant contribution given labeled workflow-performance data is expensive to collect.

Comprehensive experimental suite: main accuracy/utility comparison, ablations, OOD generalization (cross-system and cross-domain), comparison against few-shot LLM predictors, resource/cost analysis, and downstream workflow-optimization case studies.
Clear positioning relative to closely related work (FLORA-Bench, MAS-GPT) with an explicit comparison table clarifying the paper's distinguishing design choices.
Reproducibility statement and code release; detailed pseudocode (Algorithm 1) and implementation details are provided.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the core contribution largely combines existing ideas (multi-view/multi-modal fusion, contrastive+reconstruction pretraining, attention pooling) already common in NAS predictor literature and applies them to a new but structurally similar problem (as also acknowledged by building directly on FLORA-Bench's benchmark and graph construction).

Absolute performance gains over strong baselines are modest (average +1.61% accuracy, +2.79% utility; some per-domain gains near or below 1%, e.g., CodeGD +0.09%, ReasonAF utility is actually -0.35%), and reported standard deviations in Table 3 sometimes overlap with these differences, raising questions about the practical/statistical significance of the improvements.
Evaluation relies on a single benchmark (FLORA-Bench); the paper's own limitations section admits the lack of an independently curated benchmark, limiting generalizability claims.

The downstream workflow-optimization results (Table 13, §B.7) show inconsistent behavior — e.g., substantially degraded performance on HotpotQA transfer (13.37% vs. 16-21% for weaker baselines) — that is not adequately analyzed or explained, undermining the practical utility argument.

The predictor-guided search integration is minimal (random sampling + ranking), so the paper does not convincingly demonstrate end-to-end benefits of the predictor within a realistic search algorithm (e.g., evolutionary or RL-based search used by GPTSwarm/AFlow/ADAS), despite motivating the work with search efficiency.

Ablation of architectural components is incomplete — e.g., the cross-view self-attention and view-attention pooling modules within the graph encoder are not separately ablated from the multi-graph input choice, making it hard to isolate which specific architectural element drives gains.
GNN backbone ablation (Table 8) shows no single backbone dominates across domains, suggesting some fragility/inconsistency in the claimed architecture-agnostic robustness.

Baselines for performance prediction are all generic graph encoders reused from the benchmark paper; no comparison to more recent/specialized workflow predictors beyond FLORA-Bench and MAS-GPT is included as a direct predictor baseline.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: expensive trial-and-error evaluation in agentic workflow search, motivated by an interesting analogy to NAS performance predictors.
The multi-view encoding idea (graph/structural, code, and prompt/textual views) is a sensible and reasonably well-motivated extension over the single-view GNN baseline (FLORA-Bench).

Extensive set of supplementary analyses are provided: ablations on views and graph encoding, sensitivity to different LLM backbones and GNN backbones, OOD/cross-system/cross-domain generalization, label-efficiency curves, comparison against few-shot LLM predictors, resource/cost analysis, and workflow-optimization/reward-function experiments.
Reasonably thorough reproducibility effort (algorithm pseudocode, hyperparameter details, anonymized code repository, fixed seeding scheme).
weaknesses: Evaluation relies on a single benchmark (FLORA-Bench); while the paper notes it is the only public benchmark of this kind, this severely limits confidence in generalizability of the reported gains to other agentic-workflow settings.

Performance improvements over baselines are frequently small and inconsistent: several individual cells in Table 3 (e.g., ReasonAF utility) show Agentic Predictor underperforming a baseline (GCN), and many gains are within a percentage point or two, raising questions about practical significance given the reported variance.

Technical novelty is incremental: the method largely combines existing components (GNNs, cross-view attention pooling, MLP encoders, contrastive/reconstruction pretraining objectives) that are individually well established in the NAS/representation-learning literature, rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism specific to agentic workflows.

The most practically relevant demonstration—predictor-guided workflow optimization (§B.6)—is relegated to the appendix and only tested with a single simple search strategy (random search + top-k ranking), despite the paper's claim of being "search-agnostic"; no experiments validate integration with more sophisticated search/optimization algorithms actually used in prior agentic-workflow-search papers (e.g., AFlow, ADAS, GPTSwarm).

Dataset sizes for several splits are quite small (e.g., 30–42 workflows for AFlow-based subsets), raising concerns about overfitting and the robustness of both the ablation conclusions and the OOD generalization claims drawn from these subsets.

The benefit of the proposed cross-domain unsupervised pretraining (Agentic Predictor+) appears modest in the low-label regime shown in Figure 3 (roughly 73% vs. ~70% at a 0.1 label ratio), which is a less compelling improvement than the framing in the text suggests.

The predictor is restricted to binary pass/fail labels (acknowledged as a limitation), which likely constrains its usefulness for finer-grained workflow comparison and real-world deployment where partial credit or continuous metrics matter.
